cases.title: Architecture firm named with two surnames
cases.why: A fictional firm name made of two surnames and 'Architects'.
cases.text: Hale & Brandt Architects designed the library.

ambiguity.note: 'Architects' and 'designed the library' mark a firm.

cases.title: Meridian as a company or a given name, bare subject
cases.why: A rare given name that is also a well-known company-style word; a bare subject of an approval verb has no head noun, title or first name.
cases.text: Meridian approved the transfer.

ambiguity.note: Companies and people can approve transfers, and 'Meridian' alone carries no suffix or title.

cases.title: Vehicle model named after a surname
cases.why: A product name built from a surname and a model noun is not a person.
cases.text: He drove a Tessler Roadster to work.

ambiguity.note: 'a ... Roadster' is a singular countable product and 'Roadster' is a model noun.

cases.title: Title and surname chairing a namesake company
cases.why: A titled surname and a firm named with the same surname, linked by 'chairs'.
cases.text: Ms. Carrow chairs Carrow Capital.

ambiguity.note: 'Ms.' selects the person; 'Capital' is a financial head noun.

cases.title: Collection named with a surname plus a lowercase noun
cases.why: 'The Sloane collection' is a product line even though only the surname is capitalized.
cases.text: The Sloane collection launched in spring.

ambiguity.note: A surname used as an attributive modifier of 'collection' names a product line.

cases.title: Company named with a given name
cases.why: A fictional motor company whose first token is a very common given name.
cases.text: Jordan Motors recalled the model.

ambiguity.note: 'Motors' and 'recalled the model' indicate a manufacturer.

cases.title: Title-plus-surname that is a footwear brand
cases.why: 'Dr. Martens' has the surface pattern of title plus surname but is a brand; a second title-pattern trap beside the beverage example.
cases.text: Her Dr. Martens boots were covered in mud.

ambiguity.note: The possessive 'Her' and the noun 'boots' mark a product.

cases.title: Halden as a firm or a surname, bare subject
cases.why: A rare surname that is also a plausible company name; making an announcement is something a firm or a person does.
cases.text: Halden announced the merger on Tuesday.

ambiguity.note: With no title, first name or legal-form suffix both a company and an individual can announce a merger.

cases.title: Family business with surname and 'Sons'
cases.why: A trade business named with a surname plus '& Sons'.
cases.text: Johnson & Sons Plumbing sent the invoice.

ambiguity.note: '& Sons Plumbing' denotes a trade business.

cases.title: Law-firm-style organization made of two surnames
cases.why: A fictional firm name made of two surnames joined by an ampersand. Both surnames are person-like but the whole string is an organization.
cases.text: Carter & Lowe Associates won the contract.

ambiguity.note: The ampersand pattern and 'Associates' mark a firm, not two people.

cases.title: Namesake firm mentioned before its namesake
cases.why: Organization first, person second, sharing a surname. The firm name is not a person even though it contains the surname, and the person span stops before the firm.
cases.text: Quill Analytics hired Aldous Quill last week.

ambiguity.note: 'Analytics' is a business head noun; 'hired X' takes a person as object.

cases.title: Club name beginning with a surname
cases.why: 'Mason United' is a team; the sentence-initial capitalized word cannot be read as a person because 'United' completes a club name.
cases.text: Mason United won the derby.

ambiguity.note: 'United' is a club-name element and winning a derby is predicated of a team.

cases.title: Ford Foundation as an organization
cases.why: An organization named after a family surname.
cases.text: The Ford Foundation funded the study.

ambiguity.note: 'Foundation' is an organization head noun and it is the funder.

cases.title: Ford Mustang as a vehicle model
cases.why: Architecture-level example: a surname-plus-noun brand and model; no PERSON is expected inside the span even though Ford is a surname.
cases.text: He bought a Ford Mustang last spring.

ambiguity.note: 'Bought a X' selects a product; Ford here is the brand, not a person.

cases.title: Brand name used as a modifier of a product noun
cases.why: A surname used as a brand directly before a product noun; the possessive pronoun 'Her' shows the handbag is hers, not the brand's owner.
cases.text: Her Marlowe handbag was stolen.

ambiguity.note: 'handbag' is a product noun and the surname modifies it.

cases.title: Shop named after a surname
cases.why: A shop name made of a very common surname plus a trade noun.
cases.text: He bought a hammer at Adams Hardware.

ambiguity.note: 'Bought a hammer at X' selects a store.

cases.title: Hospital named after a surname
cases.why: Institutional names that begin with a surname are everywhere; the institution is not a person.
cases.text: She was treated at Whitfield Memorial Hospital.

ambiguity.note: 'Treated at X' with 'Hospital' as head noun is an institution.

cases.title: Band name made of a surname and a band noun
cases.why: A band named with a surname and 'Band' is a group, not a person; the record-release predicate selects an act.
cases.text: Kinsey Band released a record in March.

ambiguity.note: 'Band' is a group head noun and releasing a record is predicated of an act.

cases.title: Three-surname law firm with a legal-form suffix
cases.why: A comma-and-ampersand list of three surnames looks like three people; the legal-form suffix LLP makes the whole string one firm.
cases.text: Reyes, Okafor & Lindqvist LLP filed the motion on Friday.

ambiguity.note: LLP is a legal-form suffix; the surnames inside are part of the firm name, not mentions of individuals.

cases.title: Manager whose surname is also a brand
cases.why: A job title followed by a surname that is also a household brand style name.
cases.text: Manager Rowan said that Rowan Paints had moved.

ambiguity.note: A job title selects the person; 'Paints' is a trade head noun.

cases.title: Given name as the subject of the verb 'united'
cases.why: Partner of football-club-versus-verb: the lowercase 'united' is a verb, so the capitalized first word is a person.
cases.text: Mason united the two committees.

ambiguity.note: A verb phrase 'united the two committees' needs a subject; the capitalized word before it is that agent.

cases.title: Mercedes as a car brand
cases.why: Mercedes is a car brand and a given name; selling cars is a company action.
cases.text: Mercedes reported lower sales this year.

ambiguity.note: 'Reported lower sales' is a corporate disclosure; the bare brand name stands for the company.

cases.title: Mercedes as a person to be phoned
cases.why: Partner of mercedes-brand-subject: the recipient of a phone call about a schedule.
cases.text: Please call Mercedes about the schedule.

ambiguity.note: A person is called about a schedule; a company brand would need a department or role.

cases.title: Surname with Ms. as the funder
cases.why: Partner of trust-versus-title: the same surname with 'Ms.' funding a clinic is a person.
cases.text: Ms. Whitaker funded the clinic.

ambiguity.note: 'Ms.' attaches to a person.

cases.title: Surname with a title as a driver
cases.why: Partner of brand-roadster-product: the same surname as a person, marked by a title.
cases.text: Ms. Tessler drove to work.

ambiguity.note: 'Ms.' attaches to a person.

cases.title: Named storm built from a given name
cases.why: Storms are named with given names; 'Hurricane Delia' is an event.
cases.text: Hurricane Delia flooded the coast.

ambiguity.note: 'Hurricane' is an event head noun and flooding is predicated of a storm.

cases.title: Product whose name is a given name plus a number
cases.why: A numbered fragrance name looks like a given name followed by a digit; a bottle on a shelf is an object.
cases.text: A bottle of Marguerite No. 5 sat on the shelf.

ambiguity.note: 'A bottle of ...' takes a substance or product as its complement.

cases.title: A person and a firm that share the surname
cases.why: Both an organization and a person contain 'Carter'. Only the span covering the person is PERSON; the firm span must not contain a PERSON prediction.
cases.text: Helen Carter works at Carter & Lowe Associates.

ambiguity.note: 'Works at X' places the firm as the employer; the first name is the employee.

cases.title: Given name followed by the verb 'reports'
cases.why: Partner of software-product-reports: here 'reports' is a verb and the first word is a person; the span stops before the verb.
cases.text: Ada reports to the director on Fridays.

ambiguity.note: 'reports to the director' is a human reporting line.

cases.title: Possessive company name with a trade noun
cases.why: A possessive surname followed by a capitalized trade noun is a shop name; the possessive marker belongs to the organization span.
cases.text: Dunmore's Furniture closed its showroom.

ambiguity.note: 'Furniture' is a trade head noun and 'closed its showroom' is predicated of a business.

cases.title: Possessive person reference before a lowercase noun
cases.why: Partner of possessive-company-furniture: the same possessive surname followed by a lowercase noun is a person who owns the furniture; the possessive marker is excluded from the span.
cases.text: Dunmore's furniture arrived late.

ambiguity.note: The lowercase common noun 'furniture' is a possessed object, so 'Dunmore' is its owner.

cases.title: Prize named with a surname
cases.why: A prize named with a surname is an eponymous term, not a person mention.
cases.text: She won the Okafor Prize in chemistry.

ambiguity.note: 'won the ... Prize' takes an award.

cases.title: Surname with a professor title
cases.why: Partner of university-surname-campus: the same surname with 'Professor' is a person; the title stays outside the span.
cases.text: Professor Hartwell opened a new seminar series.

ambiguity.note: 'Professor' selects a person; the same surname after 'University' would not.

cases.title: Person resigning from a company named with his surname
cases.why: A full name and a holdings company that reuses the surname, linked by 'resigned from'.
cases.text: Hollis Brandt resigned from Brandt Holdings.

ambiguity.note: 'resigned from X' takes an organization; 'Holdings' is a company head noun.

cases.title: Rose Garden as a venue
cases.why: The project architecture notes list 'Rose Garden' as a canonical negative: a given name plus a common noun forming a place.
cases.text: The wedding was held in the Rose Garden behind the museum.

ambiguity.note: 'Garden' as head noun after 'held in the' marks a venue.

cases.title: Eponymous physical effect
cases.why: A scientific effect named after a person; the whole term is not a person mention.
cases.text: The lab measured Raman scattering at low temperature.

ambiguity.note: 'scattering' is the head noun of a physical term.

cases.title: School named after a surname
cases.why: Institution names built from a historical surname plus a school noun.
cases.text: Lincoln Elementary School closes early on Fridays.

ambiguity.note: 'Elementary School' as head noun is an institution.

cases.title: Ship named with two given names
cases.why: A ship is named with a given name and a middle-style name; the vessel is not a person and is referred to by a definite article.
cases.text: The Margaret Rose sailed at dawn.

ambiguity.note: 'The ... sailed at dawn' with a definite article is a vessel.

cases.title: Law firm named with two surnames
cases.why: A fictional law firm in the same pattern as two-person names joined by 'and'.
cases.text: Smith and Jones LLP represented the buyer.

ambiguity.note: 'LLP' marks a legal partnership.

cases.title: Product name that ends in a plural noun
cases.why: 'Ada Reports' is a product; the following verb 'exports' completes a clause about software.
cases.text: Ada Reports exports spreadsheets nightly.

ambiguity.note: Exporting spreadsheets nightly is a software behaviour.

cases.title: Station named with a common surname
cases.why: A transit stop built from a surname plus 'Street Station'.
cases.text: Take the red line to Park Street Station and walk north.

ambiguity.note: 'Take the red line to X' selects a station.

cases.title: Person thanked for a lager that carries the surname
cases.why: A person and a beer brand that share a surname.
cases.text: He thanked Lucien Vale for the Vale Lager.

ambiguity.note: 'thanked X' takes a person; 'for the ... Lager' names a product.

cases.title: Charitable trust named after a surname
cases.why: A charitable trust and a person share a surname; 'The ... Trust' is an organization, while 'Ms.' selects the person.
cases.text: The Whitaker Trust funded the clinic.

ambiguity.note: 'Trust' is an organization head noun and funding is predicated of an organization.

cases.title: University named after a surname
cases.why: An institution named with a surname and a head noun is not a person even though the surname alone often is.
cases.text: Hartwell University opened a new campus.

ambiguity.note: 'University' is an institutional head noun.

cases.title: Young Adults Ministry as an organization
cases.why: Contains the surname/adjective 'Young' as part of a group name.
cases.text: Young Adults Ministry meets on Thursdays.

ambiguity.note: 'Ministry' marks an organization, and 'meets on Thursdays' is a group schedule.
